To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

multiparity evaluations of calving ease (1) were estimated from a sire-MGS multiparity analysis of Holstein data, (2) were correlated at 0.79 with first-parity evaluations from a single-parity sire-MGS analysis, (3) were correlated at >0.90 with evaluations from the USDA CE evaluation, (4) were available in January 2009, and (5) are available for use in national genetic evaluations.

the multiparity evaluation of calvability has the following advantages over current USDA evaluations: 1) it is based on more records; 2) it is more accurate because it is less biased and less variable; and 3) it accounts for genetic differences between first and later calvings, and therefore, it will be more useful for selection of cows.

genetic differences between first and later parity calving performance can be evaluated separately for calving traits, and the evaluations should become more stable over time as the portion of observations from different parity changes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic evaluation of calving traits.
the evaluation of bulls for calving ease and for stillbirth.
developing a more accurate evaluation of calving traits that will be useful to breeders and dairy farmers.

multiparity evaluations for CE and SB should be used in national evaluations.

multiparity evaluations for CE and SB have been developed that will provide improved accuracies of evaluations and more stable evaluations for the lifetime of a bull.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
multiparity evaluations for CE and SB have been developed and that the multiparity evaluations are highly correlated with the national evaluations.
the multiparity evaluation of calvings is a useful addition to current evaluation procedures.

multiparity evaluations for calving ease and for stillbirth are now available.
the current evaluations are not optimal for use in the net merit index.
